And for those folks wondering why anything to the zeroth (zeroeth?) power yields one here’s a quick explanation sans formulae:

Let’s use 4 as our base and catalog what happens as we move from 4^1 to 4^2 (16) to 4^3 (64).

Each time we bump the exponent up by one, we multiply by the base (4).

Now let’s run the experiment in reverse…

Each time we bump the exponent _down_ by one we _divide_ by the base.

Therefore, moving from 4^1 to 4^0 must mean we divide 4 by 4 and *arrive at 1*.

Note that this will happen regardless of the base you chose! Mathematicians love to do that whole generalization thing.

@Tom Historically, I believe exponents were first used with positive integer powers, and negative and zero powers came along in a way that made the laws of exponents consistent in exactly the way the other commenters explain.

Alternatively, I think the way I was taught in university was by first defining the exponential function (which has base e) as the unique function that is everywhere equal to its own derivative, and letting exponentiation generally follow from that.

We are first taught with good reason that x^y means "y repeated multiplications of x" because it is well-motivated, intuitive, and applicable to basic concepts in geometry, etc. But strictly speaking this is not a proper definition of exponentiation at all, since it only works for positive integers. x^0 is usually the first example we learn where it is not directly useful, so it sticks out. But it's equally insufficient, for example, for fractional exponents, like we encounter with compounding interest, etc..

In short, there's no point in trying to wrap your head around "zero repeated multiplications of nine", which doesn't necessarily make sense. Instead, understand the rules of exponents, how they make exponentiation a useful tool, and how x^0=1 is consistent with those rules.

I'm taking another shot at explaining why n^0=1. Here we go:
n^j = n multiplied by itself k times. 
So n^3=n x n x n.
and n^2=n x n.
Similarly, n^5=n x n x n x n x n. 
You can group this as (n x n x n) • (n x n)
So (EXAMPLE A) n^5=n^3 × n^2 
and more generally, n^j × n^k=n^(j+k).
《Hang tough, we're almost done.》
If multiplying terms like n^j can be done by adding their exponents, then dividing is similarly done by /subtracting/ exponents.
So n^5 ÷ n^3 = n^2. (This is just Example A after we divided both sides by n^3.)
But then what happens when we divide any quantity by itself? We know that's always 1.
So (EXAMPLE B)  n^5 ÷ n^5 = 1.
But the two exponents here are identical.
So, 5-5 = 0. (We're dividing the base terms, so we're subtracting exponents.)
So n^5 ÷ n^5 = n^(5-5) = n^0 = 1.
And this applies to any number.

There ya go. Thanks for your patience.

@Tom For positive exponents, you multiply; for negative ones, you divide 1/(the number).  3^2 is 3x3; 3^(-2) is 1/(3x3), or 1/9. When you multiply two numbers with exponents, you add the exponents.  3^2 x 3^(-2) = 9 x 1/9 = 9/9 = 3^0 = 1.
